newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - More listless range-trading.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - More listless range-trading.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries look to continue trading in narrow ranges on Thursday, although the near-term outlook for bond prices is still negative.

Market participants said supply is once again weighing on the market, especially corporate supply. Treasuries fell on Wednesday as US West Inc reported it planned to sell $3.5 billion of notes and bonds from five years to 100 years. And more corporate issuance is slated this week, which will further pressure Treasuries, as players sell government securities to buy the new corporates, deemed more attractive.

In addition to the corporate supply, the Treasury will sell more than $100 billion in bills, notes and bonds in the next six weeks. Wednesday, Treasury said it would sell $17.5 billion two-year notes Tuesday and $12.5 billion five-year notes next Wednesday. Traders noted, though, that the market is being controlled by just a few small accounts.

"There is plenty of paper, but customers are not putting money to work," said Bill Kirby, a trader at Prudential Securities Inc. "People are comfortable and content to wait until yields move a little higher, which will happen because there is a lot of supply."
Bond yields are expected to rise to seven percent, or higher, players said, but it might take a few weeks as more economic news shows a stronger economy.
Due on Thursday are weekly jobless claims data at 0830 EST/1330 GMT and the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia's business outlook survey for January is scheduled for release at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.
Claims are seen down 6,000 to 355,000 in the week ended January 11, according to a Reuters poll. The Philadelphia Fed's main diffussion index is seen rising to 4.8 from December's -2.2.
The data are not expected to move the market significantly, as most players are waiting for Friday's industrial production data.
Kirby said the production numbers should be strong, which will "put pressure on the market and yields will go up."
Players said the recent downtrade does not look to end soon, as rallies are seen as good opportunities to sell and book profits.
Traders said the market will also keep an eye on surging European markets, especially Bunds. If Bunds continue to do well, Treasuries will look even cheaper, and entice buying.
The 30-year bond closed at 96-8/32, down 9/32, to yield 6.79 percent. The two-year note was up 1/32 at 99-20/32 to yield 5.95 percent.
Federal funds are seen opening at the 5-1/4 percent target rate to 5-5/16 percent on Thursday.
